Course.title: Phase 1
Course.description: The initial offering leaving Courses to allow for future content

Lesson.title: What is the IPA?
Lesson.description: In this module, you’ll learn what this course is about, what the IPA is and how it’s used, and what it looks like.

Lesson.title: Why the IPA?
Lesson.description: In this module, you’ll learn why the IPA is a useful tool for learning dialects and accents when compared to the English spelling system, and the difference between a dialect and accent.

Lesson.title: The Final Pitch
Lesson.description: In this module, you’ll learn what to expect from the rest of this instructional video series.

Lesson.title: Rethinking Speech
Lesson.description: In this module, you’ll learn about the physiology of verbal communication, the difference between a vowel and a consonant, and elements of a dialect other than pronunciation.

Lesson.title: Consonants
Lesson.description: In this module, you’ll learn about the formation of consonants within a General American dialect, and their corresponding IPA symbols.

Lesson.title: Vowels
Lesson.description: In this module, you’ll learn about the formation of one-part vowels (monophthongs) within a General American dialect, and their corresponding IPA symbols.

Lesson.title: Diphthongs & Triphtongs
Lesson.description: In this module, you’ll learn about the formation of two and three-part vowels (diphthongs and triphthongs) within a General American dialect, and their corresponding IPA symbols.

Lesson.title: Transcription Concepts
Lesson.description: In this module, you’ll learn about some of the best practices when transcribing in the IPA.

Lesson.title: Transcription In Action
Lesson.description: In this module, you’ll learn about transcribing phrases and sentences in the context of connected speech, including how to incorporate essential diacritic and suprasegmental markings.

Lesson.title: Stress
Lesson.description: In this module, you will learn the difference between lexical and operative stress, and how to indicate stress in your IPA transcription.

Lesson.title: Fake Lexical Chart
Lesson.description: In this module, you will learn how to utilize a lexical template through the creation of a fake dialect; and in the instructional materials you’ll learn how to analyze your personal idiolect.

Lesson.title: Gathering Resources
Lesson.description: In this module, you’ll learn what makes an example speaker resource high quality, and how to categorize them into primary, secondary, and tertiary resources.

Lesson.title: Segmental Features of the Dialect
Lesson.description: In this module, you’ll learn about all of the segmental features, or one-to-one sound changes, of a British Received Pronunciation Dialect when compared to a General American Dialect.

Lesson.title: Distinct Features of the Dialect
Lesson.description: In this module, you will learn about certain distinct features within the British RP dialect, including the linking and intrusive “R”, the “liquid-U”, and syncope.

Lesson.title: Prosody of the Dialect
Lesson.description: In this module, you will learn about the prosody, or musical elements, of a British RP dialect.

Lesson.title: Transcription Transformation
Lesson.description: In this module, we will begin the process of transcribing “Hamlet’s Advice” into British RP. You’ll be tasked with completing the transcription for homework.

Lesson.title: Performance Implementation
Lesson.description: In this final module, you’ll learn about the suggested steps to marry your dialect work to your performance choices.

Lesson.title: Dialect Transcription in Action
Lesson.description: In this module, you will learn about the order of operations to undergo when transcribing your text from one dialect into another, along with some helpful tips and tricks.

Lesson.title: Outro
Lesson.description: Congratulations on completing The Actor's Guide to IPA and Accents!

Lesson.title: Checkpoint 1
Lesson.description: During the following exercises, you’ll put what you’ve learned so far to the test.

AnswerOption.feedback: The <W> in “question” is often considered an “voiceless labial-velar fricative”, or more simply, an “unvoiced W”, which looks like this: [ʍ]. It’s rarely used on its own in GenAm, but often appears directly after unvoiced plosive consonants within the same syllable. Others examples: “twice” /tʍaɪ̆s/, “queen” /kʍin/.

Similar to “voiceless [ʍ]”, in GenAm the approximate [ɹ] is devoiced after a voiceless plosive consonant within the same syllable, which is denoted with this diacritic beneath the symbol: [ ̥ ]. Other examples include: “prime” /pɹ̥aɪ̆m/, “trace” /tɹ̥eɪ̆s/

Similar to “devoiced [ɹ̥]”, in GenAm the approximate [l] is devoiced after a voiceless plosive consonant within the same syllable, which is denoted with this diacritic beneath the symbol: [ ̥ ].  Other examples include: “climb” /kl̥aɪ̆m/, “pleasure” /pl̥ɛʒɚ/
